title: A New Antibiotic Idea From An Old Source
body_text: As longtime readers will know, I am always ready to celebrate advances in antibiotic research. That’s for several good reasons, not least of which is that such advances are notoriously hard to come by. And of course they’re also extremely important from a public health perspective: we are under constant threat from pathogenic infections, and the organisms that cause them are getting steadily more resistant to our existing treatments. At this point the only people in the industrialized world who know what it looks like to be without antibiotics are those who have studied history - and let me tell you, it will curl your hair. No, we need these drugs very much, and we need better ones. So this new paper is welcome indeed. Its multinational team of authors have done a close study of bacterial natural products in the hopes of finding overlooked compounds, and rather surprisingly they have a really good example. Streptomyces rimosus is the soil bacterium that produces the very well-known antibiotic oxytetracycline. That one was first described in 1950, from the bacterium that was isolated from a soil sample not far from Pfizer’s labs (those were the days!) And it’s been in constant use ever since, with all that entails. But S. rimosus has more to offer, it turns out. The team has put together a fractionation and analysis platform for natural product isolates that is designed at every point to reject known antibiotics and to prioritize compounds with what seem to be new modes of action or activity spectra. In this case, this yielded a set of active fractions from an S. rimosus culture, many of which did contain tetracycline structures. But not all of them! Two fractions showed unusual mass spectral signatures, and activity-based purification (a painstaking process) narrowed down on a family of cyclic peptides that have been dubbed the manikomycins (from a Hindi/Punjabi word (mani) for a precious gemstone). The most abundant - a relative term! - was a nonapeptide deemed manikomycin A. It’s cyclized via an ester linkage between the C-terminal His residue and the side-chain OH of another threonine. And it’s a very unusual beast, because it includes a run of D-amino acids (the unnatural stereochemical series), with three D-arginine residues, a D-asparagine, a D-phenylalanine, and a D-ornithine which is an amino acid that’s not even found in many species (outside of birds) in much quantity. This is obviously assembled by nonribosomal peptide synthetase enzymes, because no ribosome would put up with such building blocks. The authors identified the biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) and were able to transfer it completely into a different strain of Streptomyces, which then began producing the exact same suite of compounds. So how does it work as an antibiotic? There are plenty of charged amino acids in there, so the first thought was that it did something to bacterial membranes. But this didn’t seem to be the case on closer inspection. A search for targets inside the bacterial cells was undertaken by passaging good ol’ E. coli over and over with low concentrations of the antibiotic, which is a classic technique to find which proteins respond to the pressure by being mutated over time. Wild-type strains were very susceptible, which is nice to see, but eventually that got up to strains that were up to 32x more resistant. One of these showed mutations in some membrane peptide transporters (which makes sense), but another seemed to become resistant through mutations in a particular large ribosomal subunit protein. That was the key. It turns out that the manikomycins are indeed bacterial protein synthesis inhibitors, but through a mechanism that has never been seen before in such an antibiotic. It binds to the “E-site” of the 50S subunit, in a pocket that really doesn’t exist in eukaryotic ribosomes at all. The well-known protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide also messes with this part of the ribosome, but in a different way than the MKMs. Close study of both the sequences of abnormal proteins produced and of cryo-EM structures of the ribosomal subunit shows that the compound stalls the ribosomal function in several ways depending on the structure of the protein that’s being produced. And the team was also able to track down how S. rimosus itself manages to avoid being killed by its own antibiotic, through a peculiar methylation enzyme that goes after the ribose of cytidine residues and allows protein synthesis to continue without stalling. The gene for this protein is found only in strains that have the biosynthesis genes for the manikomycins; it’s a very tight story indeed. Manikomycin A itself is not going to be a wonder drug, though. It has activity against select species of Gram-negative bacteria as well as mycobacteria, but strikes out against a number of other Gram-negatives and against most all of the Gram-positives. This includes many types where its binding site is conserved, so lack of activity is likely due to poor uptake, likely due to lack of the transporter proteins it likes to use. The compound seems to be nontoxic to rodents, but its pharmacokinetics need work (rapid clearance). The good news is that the scaffold looks open to a lot of relatively straightforward chemical modifications, and that is certainly going to be a big effort. A new binding site on the bacterial ribosome is worth it!
